a6328.speech: The World Bank report also insists on transparency in debt management as a lever of performance. ; Another major trend highlighted in the report is the rise of multilateral institutions as a source of development financing: between 2012 and 2023, net multilateral debt inflows to IDA-eligible countries rose from 6 to 20 billion dollars, while bilateral and private creditors largely reduced their exposure in the region.

a6328.speaker: World Bank
a6328.speech: For the World Bank, recent efforts on budget consolidation and restructuring are encouraging, but insufficient in the medium term; the pressures remain strong: heavy bond maturities, the contraction of foreign aid, rate volatility.

a6440.speaker: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
a6440.speech: Has disclosed that it provided humanitarian assistance valued at $200,000 to flood victims in Bauchi State.

a6440.speaker: ECOWAS Directorate of Humanitarian and Social Affairs, led by Dr. Sintiki Tarfa-Ugbe
a6440.speech: Said it has extended significant humanitarian aid to 2024 flood victims in Bauchi State in Nigeria as part of its Emergency Flood Response Project to alleviate the hardship caused by the flood.

a6440.speaker: ECOWAS (statement)
a6440.speech: A statement by ECOWAS said: "the efforts which targeted six Local Government Areas, saw 1,000 households across the six Local Government Areas—Katagum, Jama'are, Zaki, Gamawa, Giade, and Kirfe, receiving package that includes a cash transfer of 75,000 naira per household, along with food and non-food items. Valued at $200,000, the initiative targets 1,000 households across six Local Government Areas—Katagum, Jama'are, Zaki, Gamawa, Giade, and Kirfe—offering vital relief to those impacted by the devastating floods. Beneficiaries are received a package that includes a cash transfer of 75,000 naira per household, along with food and non-food items. The distribution of relief materials in Bauchi, which commenced on December 15, 2024, is designed to mitigate the hardships caused by the floods, provide immediate relief, and foster resilience among the affected communities."

a6502.speaker: Danicius Kaihenneh Sengbeh, Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) Communication Manager
a6502.speech: Explained that the Authority is making steady progress toward meeting its domestic revenue targets: “I am pleased to inform you that out of the 804.6 million United States dollars, as of the 13th of July, the LRA had been able to collect an estimated amount of 422 million,” he stated in a phone interview on OK FM on Tuesday, July 15, 2025 ; noted that despite economic and logistical challenges the LRA is “moving significantly well” and is optimistic about reaching the year-end goal ; projected an even more promising future, stating, “Looking at the trend, the LRA is going to hit a billion [in annual revenue]” ; emphasised the need for an improved national tax system, sustained public awareness campaigns, and stronger stakeholder support to enhance compliance and enforcement.

a6623.speaker: World Health Organisation
a6623.speech: In mid-August, declared the mpox outbreak a "public health emergency of international concern".

a6623.speaker: Public Citizen, US advocacy group
a6623.speech: Says it fears "that Bavarian Nordic may be exploiting the latest global health crisis, putting profits over people". If the company would share its technology with factories in low and middle-income countries, the group says, the price could be slashed.

a6623.speaker: Bavarian Nordic
a6623.speech: The company won't share its technology with factories in low and middle-income countries. It claims that's not how its business model works. Instead, it is encouraging rich governments to buy full-priced vaccines and then donate them.

a6623.speaker: Campaigners
a6623.speech: Campaigners are clear - both Bavarian Nordic and KM Biologics must share their research with other manufacturers to increase supply and bring prices down.

a6623.speaker: Spain (government pledge)
a6623.speech: Pledged to donate 500,000 doses from its own stockpile.

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On the economic trend for 2025: “The world is living through a very complex moment of great uncertainty. And everything that happens in the world has an impact on our little crumb, on our little grain of earth that we are here in Cabo Verde.” He said the macroeconomic variables have performed well, with substantial improvements after the blow of Covid, which in 2020 meant a contraction of the economy of 20.8%, and that the outlook is positive/moderate. “We are a micro country, a micro-economy, dispersed, with vulnerabilities and very dependent on certain sectors, as the Covid and post-Covid crisis itself revealed.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On planning amid uncertainty: “As we are enclosed in a very particular reality and there is knowledge and experience of the country, it is possible to plan, there always being unforeseen events that can happen. Of course we are impacted by what happens in the world, in particular in Europe, in foreign trade, in foreign direct investment, in the origin of tourists, in remittances, to which those from the USA are added. By nature the businessman has to be optimistic, with his feet on the ground, that is, realistic and pragmatic.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On the macroeconomic picture: said the country’s economic performance has been relatively robust in recent years after growth of only about 1% on average between 2009 and 2015; in 2016 the growth rate was 4.3% and average annual growth between 2016 and 2019 was 4.9%, reaching about 7% in 2019 (IMF data). In 2020, with COVID, “we suffered the greatest economic contraction in our history (-22.8%), the second largest contraction in Africa”. In 2023 the country returned to 5.1%. He noted public debt reached “stratospheric” levels above 150% of GDP and fell to 110% of GDP in 2024, “which reveals a remarkable recovery”; inflation rose to 5.4% in 2021 with a peak of 7.6% in 2022, returning to 1.3% in 2023 with an estimate of 2% for 2024. “I would say that in macroeconomic terms, and for now, things are going well.” He added that risks and constraints remain, “knowing that we have significant fringes of the population in a situation below the minimum conditions of human dignity.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On the construction sector: said the sector remains relevant in the economy, with a weight of about 10% of GDP and in the volume of employment it generates. As president of ACEC he highlighted two relevant issues: (a) “The sector was badly battered by the high inflation that followed post-Covid and worsened with the war in Ukraine and companies were confronted with a dizzying increase in materials, energy and transport. The problem is that public works are at a fixed, non-revisable price.” A temporary law was eventually approved allowing companies to mitigate the additional costs; (b) “The public Works Owner should make a greater investment in the technical improvement of the projects put out to public tender. A deficient execution project always brings problems to the works owner and in particular to the executing company... A good project is always half the road travelled in executing a work.” He said this still happens too often and must be corrected.

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On interest rates and company financing: cited a sectoral study on the financial system covering 2015 to 2023 prepared by PD Consult, of Paulino Dias, and said “very sincerely, and unless for some other reason that escapes me, I do not see that it brings any major problems other than a slight pressure for a rise in the interest rates charged by the banks to companies and families.” He explained that changes in the BCV’s key rates historically do not lead to major changes in average lending rates; that average rates between 2015 and 2023 stayed in a narrow band close to 9%; and that the banks have returned to profits and good profitability, solvency indicators have improved much, and “healthy and profitable banks is what we all need in the economy.” “The current level of rates is good enough for the banks because it is giving them good profitability. There is no reason for those rates to be increased.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On which sectors may grow most: said tourism has an enormous weight, 25% of GDP, and guarantees 25% of formal jobs. “I would say that in 2025 that will continue to be our engine of growth, dragging all the other sectors and sub-sectors along. But in terms of changing the structure of sectoral contributions to GDP, the effects of reforms and policies are only felt in the medium term, between three and five years.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On opportunities: pointed to the World Bank’s recent 2024 study “Creating Markets in Cabo Verde”, saying the opportunities, some of them niche, are in tourism, the blue economy – or sea economy – and digital services, provided the questions of competition and the regulatory environment, transport and logistics, and energy – the major constraints – are resolved, so as to achieve a private sector, of national or international capital, with good businesses and adequate profitability.

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On the World Bank’s conclusion that the Cape Verdean development model has been exhausted since 2008: recalled a 2016 interview he gave to Expresso das Ilhas titled “We need to change the model of economic development or we will not guarantee a minimum of prosperity for all”, and noted others had said it before, “even in past decades like the late Eugénio Inocêncio, who at the beginning of the nineties had already said that we had to stop being an economy of recycling foreign aid and become a productive economy. And that continues to be Cabo Verde’s greatest challenge even today.” He described market failures and the structure of supply: monopolies in energy, ports and airport management, and duopolies in communications, water, pharmaceuticals, fuels and insurance, which “creates distortions”, increases inefficiencies, and leaves a very large weight of the state business sector, “and indeed there is no report by international institutions that habitually follow the Cape Verdean economy that does not refer to that.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On low productivity: “Here, really, I let out a big sigh. In the sense that, in the short term, I would say no.” He said the answer is to invest in human capital and education, noting positively that the Ministry of Education aims to start taking international tests assessing essential student competences, and investment in STEM areas. He pointed to the outflow of labour as a big problem for companies, worsened in recent years – “naturally those who emigrate, if they are not the most qualified, are the most active, the most ambitious, who do not mind taking risks” – as well as company organisation and management modernisation, constraints such as inter-island maritime transport, excessive dependence on imports and delayed orders causing unwanted stoppages, high factor costs, and a public administration that also has productivity problems whose inefficiency and ineffectiveness “in a way contaminates the country, the economy and companies, public or private.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On emigration of workers: “That problem is already happening. It has already happened. Those people left and it is clear that this is already – and I know it from talking with several companies in different sectors – a big problem.” He said Europe, and Portugal in particular, has had a labour deficit for some years and Portuguese employers had long pressed for easier entry, so the migration results from great demand for people; and that since emigrating in search of better living conditions is “in the genes of the Cape Verdean”, the aspiration is legitimate. “But this mass migration, it is indisputable, constitutes a problem. The bet with the greatest future possibility is for us to manage, here inside, to generate enough economy, enough income, enough companies to allow salaries to be attractive so that it does not pay to emigrate, at least in material terms. The ambition of the country, of society, should be that.”

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On needed economic reforms: “It is indisputable that this government adopted another posture in relation to the private sector, with a friendlier environment. There are some reforms under way in a positive direction. There is also a strategic vision for the country, of a platform country that provides services to the outside. If the objectives are realistic and within our capacities that vision is correct and could bring more development to the country.” He called for the state business sector to function better and deliver timely, higher-quality services; for selective infrastructure investment – “God save us from the investments made in the 2000s, many of them turned into white elephants and are weighing on our public debt” – for digital services such as fintechs, for better state treatment of foreign direct investment, and for deepening tourism with greater linkages between the big hotels and the local economy.

a6817.speaker: President of ACEC (Cape Verdean construction companies association), businessman interviewed
a6817.speech: On the biggest challenges for businesspeople in 2025: said that apart from global ones, “the usual” – inter-island transport, whether air or maritime. He gave passenger figures (2 million international passengers in 2023, surpassing the 1.9 million pre-pandemic level of 2019; 3 million total domestic and international passengers in 2024 against 2.7 million in 2019) and said that on domestic air transport “I would say we lost an opportunity with Binter, which was in the market for only a few years”, citing domestic traffic of 698,000 in 2015, 715,000 in 2016 with TACV, 959,000 in 2017, 884,000 in 2018 and 821,000 in 2019 under Binter – “the golden age in terms of domestic passengers” – falling to 249,000 in 2020 and 287,000 in 2021, then 494,000 in 2022, 549,000 in 2023 and 612,000 in 2024. He said he did not understand why the government did not take up the 30% stake foreseen in the agreement with Binter plus the option to buy 19%, called the earlier “sale” of already largely amortised ATR aircraft to the supplier and their leaseback “a ruinous option of the administration of the time, sanctioned by the government” aimed “only at making up the accounts”, and said the 30% stake “clearly should have been taken”. He added: “I usually say that this government works better in emergencies than in what is routine”, citing COVID measures and the reactivation of TACV on domestic routes as successes, while noting leased aircraft with crew is a transitional solution with unbearable costs. On maritime transport, “for me, there is an original sin in the tender that was launched: having required five practically new vessels, less than 15 years old, to operate in this market of ours which is so narrow and meagre”, saying the market did not warrant five vessels and the investment could not be amortised.

a6817.speaker: World Bank (2024 study “Creating Markets in Cabo Verde”)
a6817.speech: The World Bank in a recent 2024 study entitled “Creating Markets in Cabo Verde” makes a diagnosis of the private sector and identifies the engines of growth, the challenges and the opportunities ; the institution also said that the Cape Verdean development model has been exhausted at least since 2008 ; the institution also spoke of a problem that all Cape Verdean businesspeople have known for many years, which is the question of low productivity in Cabo Verde.

a6817.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF data)
a6817.speech: Cited as the source for the growth figures: growth of about 1% on average between 2009 and 2015, 4.3% in 2016, average annual growth of 4.9% between 2016 and 2019, and about 7% in 2019 (IMF data).

a6817.speaker: PD Consult sectoral study on the financial system (by Paulino Dias)
a6817.speech: A sectoral study was published covering an extended period, from 2015 to 2023, prepared by PD Consult, of Paulino Dias, which traces the evolution and portrays the whole and each of the banks operating in Cabo Verde in that period and helps to better understand a sector so vital to any economy.

a6817.speaker: Eugénio Inocêncio (late Cape Verdean figure)
a6817.speech: at the beginning of the nineties had already said that “we had to stop being an economy of recycling foreign aid in order to become a productive economy.”

a6817.speaker: Official figures (cited by the interviewer)
a6817.speech: According to official figures, in 2023 Portugal granted about 5,000 work visas to Cape Verdeans, more than in the previous 4 years.

a6916.speaker: USAID (official letter to contracting and agreement officers, 24 January 2025)
a6916.speech: Announced the suspension of new obligations of funds and the disbursement of funds under development objective agreements (DOAGs) until the review of USAID-funded foreign assistance programmes is completed, and instructed all officers to stop work, salaries and travel for all organisations and institutions that received assistance through the agency: "Consistent with the President's order to review and realign United States foreign assistance and additional guidance issued by the Department of State, USAID is pausing new obligations of funds and disbursement of funds under development objective agreements (DOAGs) until the review of USAID-funded foreign assistance programmes is completed."

a6916.speaker: Jami J. Rodgers, USAID Chief Acquisition Officer (Executive Director of Procurement)
a6916.speech: Explained that the decision stems from the implementation of President Trump's order to review and realign United States foreign assistance ; said the guidance includes foreign assistance through all programme accounts ("Title III") but not operating expenses and the capital investment fund account ("Title II"), and that the hold applies to funds associated with all entities receiving awards ; said contracting and agreement officers will no longer be permitted to modify, extend, or exercise options or renewals of existing funding beyond the confirmed actions: "Contracting and agreement officers should immediately issue stop-work orders, or modify or terminate existing awards in accordance with the terms and conditions of the relevant award" ; said that after the review, officers will communicate with vendors and recipients about whether an award will continue, be modified, or be terminated, and that no new awards, RFPs, RFAs or NOFOs may be issued until each activity is reviewed and approved as consistent with the President's policy ; said the Secretary of State has agreed to issue allowances from the hold for "Emergency food assistance and administrative costs, including salaries necessary to administer that assistance for a period; salaries and associated administrative costs, including travel, for all categories of personal services contractors" and "Legitimate expenses incurred before 24 January 2025 under existing awards, or legitimate expenses associated with stop-work orders, suspensions, or modifications resulting from the hold in those areas approved by the Director of foreign assistance" ; said a waiver process, together with the review of activities, will be issued shortly, within 30 days.

a6916.speaker: Executive order signed by US President Donald Trump, 20 January 2025
a6916.speech: "All department and agency heads with responsibility for United States foreign development assistance programmes shall immediately pause new obligations and disbursements of development assistance funds," the order read.

a7007.speaker: Thierno Bocar Tall, CEO of the African Biofuels and Renewable Energy Company (SABER)
a7007.speech: Gave an update on renewable energy initiatives and the new projects envisaged: said phase 1 of the Programme for the Development of Renewable Energies and Energy Efficiency (PRODERE I) allowed Benin to be equipped with solar power plants, 1,300 low-consumption streetlights and solar kits, and that to consolidate these gains a new initiative called the Solar Energy Development Programme (PROVES) is being implemented; announced that American and Algerian financing will support this vast undertaking in order to raise Benin's renewable energy capacity to 4,000 or even 5,000 Kw.

a7007.speaker: Claude Gbedonougbo Gbaguidi, president of the Energy Regulatory Authority (ARE)
a7007.speech: Gave an update on a mission ordered by the Head of State concerning the Nangbeto dam, temporarily shut down because of the works on the Athieme bridge, reporting that the company SOGEA SATOM, in charge of the works, with the support of the military engineering corps, is working so that by 15 June the bridge under construction will no longer be an obstacle to the proper functioning of the dam, which injects a total capacity of 40 Mw into the assets of Benin and Togo.

a7007.speaker: Camille Kpogbemabou, director general of the Beninese Electricity Company (SBEE)
a7007.speech: Gave an update on the deployment of prepaid meters in the public administration, confiding that 85% of state structures are already covered by the operation begun last August, while giving assurances about the corrective measures taken to meet the operation's requirements; said a vast project to switch the 500,000 conventional connections over to prepayment is under way and that 45,000 prepaid meters are already available, pending the 100,000 expected under the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA).

a7007.speaker: Gero Amoussouga, interim Minister in charge of Energy, and Alassani Tigri, Secretary General of the government
a7007.speech: Reassure the population as to the arrangements made to eradicate and durably avert the energy crisis in Benin — in the short term the rental of generators from private companies, the supply of natural gas to the Maria Gleta power plant and the implementation of the new national rural energy programme; in the medium and long term raising installed capacity to 1,500 Mw, with the $411 million of the Millennium Challenge Account and a first 120 Mw phase of a 400 Mw power plant financed by the Islamic Development Bank.

a7007.speaker: Felix Comlan Ebo
a7007.speech: Said that the solar streetlights in Cotonou's Agla neighbourhood are the first phase of the Solar Energy Development Programme (PROVES), with 650 streetlights and six mini power plants, and that the second phase, financed by the Americans, will soon be implemented for 1,500 streetlights.

a7040.speaker: Dr Charles Amadi, Principal Investigator of the Global Biotechnology Potato Partnership (GBPP)
a7040.speech: Said in an interactive session with journalists at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS), Jos: “The partnership aims to conduct field trials and regulatory assessments to ensure the safety and efficacy of the genetically modified potato varieties. It works on capacity building and training for farmers, extension workers, and regulators to support the adoption and proper management of these biotechnological innovations. The GBPP aims to improve food security by increasing potato yields and reducing crop losses due to diseases and pests. It seeks to enhance the livelihoods of smallholder farmers by providing them with more robust and productive potato varieties” ; “We are required by law to do regulatory, national performance and on-farm trials before they can be released. We have to submit dossiers from the regulatory trial to NBMA for consideration for environmental release. By eliminating late blight disease, your potato crop yield will be increased and stabilized enabling you to have more food and make more money. The late blight-resistant potato is safe and can reduce the cost of growing your potato crop by reducing the need for fungicides by 90%, this leads to less labor costs, stable yields, and better livelihood for your family. It reduces the harmful effects of fungicide use on the environment. The new variety which had so far gone one year trial is funded by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) as part of the Feed the Future Global Biotech Potato Partnership.”

a7285.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF) projections
a7285.speech: Somalia's economy, which grew 4.1 percent in 2024, is expected to slow to 3 percent in 2025 and 3.3 percent in 2026 due to foreign aid cuts and recurring climate shocks, according to IMF projections. Inflation is forecast to remain stable at 3.5 percent, though food prices are likely to remain high.

a7285.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a7285.speech: Noted that Somalia's fiscal performance has stayed broadly on track. The country's budget deficit is projected at 0.3 percent of GDP in 2025, rising slightly to 0.75 percent in 2026 as the government expands social spending and prepares for national elections.

a7285.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a7285.speech: Commended Somalia's continued reform drive, highlighting strong income tax collection under a new tax law, customs modernization, and strict control over spending.

a7285.speaker: Ran Bi, IMF Mission Chief
a7285.speech: “To mitigate the negative impact of foreign aid cuts and support their reform efforts, the authorities have requested an augmentation of access under the ECF arrangement,” said IMF Mission Chief Ran Bi, praising the Somali government's commitment to reform despite economic challenges.

a7285.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a7285.speech: Continued international support, the IMF said, remains crucial to maintain momentum amid uncertainty surrounding aid flows and worsening climate shocks.

a7285.speaker: Somali authorities
a7285.speech: Have requested an augmentation of access under the current ECF by SDR 30 million (about US$40 million) to cushion against aid disruptions and fund social programs.

a7343.speaker: Fred Byamukama, State Minister for Transport (Uganda)
a7343.speech: Speaking to NTV, stated that the government is investigating cases where individuals have tampered with digital number plates on vehicles and motorcycles, removing them, and that the government suspects some of these incidents are orchestrated by individuals connected to unlicensed garages.

a7343.speaker: Car importers
a7343.speech: Have expressed concern over the slow registration of digital plates, which has negatively impacted their businesses and, consequently, the taxes collected by the Uganda Revenue Authority from bond owners and other importers.

a7372.speaker: H.E. Sultan Abdulrahman Al-Dhakel, Ambassador of Saudi Arabia to Ghana
a7372.speech: Reaffirmed Saudi Arabia's commitment to fostering mutually beneficial relations, emphasizing the importance of collaboration for growth and development.

a7372.speaker: Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa (MP), Minister for Foreign Affairs of Ghana
a7372.speech: Expressed Ghana's gratitude for Saudi Arabia's ongoing support, particularly in education, construction, trade, and humanitarian assistance; acknowledged Saudi contributions towards aiding inner-city communities and providing relief for victims of recent floods in the Volta Region.

a7372.speaker: Both parties (Saudi Ambassador and Ghana's Foreign Affairs Minister)
a7372.speech: Reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral relations and exploring new avenues for cooperation between the two nations.

a7391.speaker: Nigeria Police Force
a7391.speech: Have warned the #FreeNnamdiKanu protesters to obey court orders restraining their planned protest on Monday.

a7391.speaker: Benjamin Hundeyin, Nigeria Police Force spokesperson
a7391.speech: In a statement on Saturday, warned against the planned protests, referring to an order issued by the Federal High Court, Abuja division, on October 17, 2025 in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/2202/2025 — Federal Republic of Nigeria v. Omoyele Sowore & 4 others; he said the order, given by M.G. Umar, restrains the respondents and others acting under their instruction from staging protests within and around Aso Rock, the National Assembly complex, force headquarters, the Court of Appeal, Eagle Square, and Shehu Shagari Way.

a7391.speaker: Federal High Court, Abuja (interim injunction, Justice M.G. Umar)
a7391.speech: Restrained human rights activist Omoyele Sowore and others from organising or participating in the planned protest seeking to strengthen calls for Kanu's release, following an ex parte application filed by the Federal Government through the Nigeria Police.

a7391.speaker: Court of Appeal / Supreme Court (rulings)
a7391.speech: In October 2022 the Court of Appeal ordered Kanu's immediate release, but the Supreme Court, on December 15, 2023, overturned the decision and permitted the Federal Government to continue his trial while he remains in detention.

a7391.speaker: Ambassador Kalu Ofon Emmanuel, Lagos State Chapter President, International Human Rights Protection Service (Naples, Florida, USA)
a7391.speech: Attributed the recent push for the release of Nnamdi Kanu to politics; speaking to Sunday Independent, revealed that both the detention and the push for the release are politically motivated, and that as political campaigns gather momentum politicians are warming up for next elections, hence the fresh push. He cited the recent presidential pardon granted those he termed world-class criminals, terrorists, drug barons, kidnappers, highway armed robbers and killers, who he said should not be seen walking freely on the roads, and wondered why Nnamdi Kanu should not be released; maintained that if the judiciary had been reliable Kanu should have been released long ago, saying those who derive joy and make merchandise from his detention should think twice as they are not invincible; indicated the fresh push is due to a rise in political activities for the 2027 general election: “The people are holding their voter cards which are their weapons and mandate. If people are not disfranchised and have free and fair elections, the wind will blow soon and their anus will be exposed.”

a7391.speaker: Rev. Dr. Felix Nwosu
a7391.speech: Speaking to Sunday Independent, attributed the fresh push for Nnamdi Kanu's release to the fact that he has been in incarceration for too long, saying his release is long overdue; said that President Tinubu's not including Kanu among those granted presidential pardon ignited the fresh push by Igbo groups and intelligentsia; added that Kanu's continued incarceration while people who committed heinous crimes are given presidential pardon has made the call for his release political, which will continue to re-echo as 2027 campaigns gather momentum; said his continued detention has reopened the cry for marginalisation of Ndigbo since after the civil war and his release will help assuage this feeling: “The recent presidential pardon that did not favour Nnamdi Kanu seems to remind Ndigbo that they are not being fairly treated as a people in Nigeria where leaders continue to profess unity, equity and fairness... The Nigerian people do not want the marginalisation of Ndigbo anymore. They want equal rights to every Nigerian person. Nigerians feel that Nnamdi Kanu should be among those released for peace to reign in South Eastern Nigeria as his continued detention has caused a lot of chaos in this part of the country. If truly we are practising federal character as being prescribed, President Tinubu should look into the case of Nnamdi Kanu for urgent consideration as a gift for Ndigbo. Although his case is still pending in court and that those who bagged presidential pardon are convicts, the president also has the power to instruct the Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice to discontinue the trial.”

a7391.speaker: Rev. Dr. Felix Nwosu
a7391.speech: Said what is needed now is negotiation and lobbying for Kanu to be granted bail, adding that “Nigerians should not forget Nnamdi Kanu's suffering as a result of leaving the country when he was granted bail for the first time”; called for serious dialogue between IPOB and the Federal Government, just as was the case in the Middle East between Hamas and Israel, for peace to reign in Nigeria, especially South Eastern Nigeria.

a7391.speaker: Hon. Charles Anike, National President, Eastern Union (EU)
a7391.speech: Said the fresh push for Nnamdi Kanu's release was due to the realisation that there was no basis or justifiable reason for his continued detention; said Kanu did not commit any known crime, “except that clueless government of APC under Buhari became too afraid of Kanu's growing influence and the awareness he was creating among the Igbos. That was reinforced by the deep seated hatred of Buhari for the Igbo race. Don't we really have a constitution? Are there no specified duration for trial of whatever allegations? Why the endless court drama? The APC virus has spread and swallowed our judiciary like other institutions, otherwise why would any judge join in the political conspiracies against Nnamdi Kanu who conducted his agitations without violence?” ; said Nigerians have seen that whatever crime the Federal Government claimed Kanu committed was also committed even more seriously and simultaneously by Sunday Igboho, who has been agitating for Oduduwa Republic: “So, why should Sunday Igboho not [be] in detention like Nnamdi Kanu, but is walking freely? There are several others in the north who indisputably have been agitating for Arewa State and they were not arrested or detained. What about those well-known terrorists that have been on a rampage in the north...? Are they not operating freely and even brandishing their weapons on viral videos? What has the Federal Government done to them? Are they not celebrities, to the extent that government officials are publicly and proudly posing in pictures with them in the name of negotiating with them? Even those of them (terrorists) that were arrested during ex-President Jonathan's era were all released by Buhari and many of them, said to be ‘repentants', allegedly enlisted into the Nigerian Army. The reason our military men have become sacrificial lambs to the Boko Haram terrorists. This is the only country in the world where terrorists are celebrated and tolerated... While hardened terrorists are roaming freely, Nnamdi Kanu will be kept in detention for years for agitating against marginalisation and injustice. The fresh push for his release is due to the realisation that Nnamdi Kanu did nothing to warrant his incarceration. Rather his detention is another way of continuing the humiliation of Ndigbo in Nigeria as a people that lost a civil war. The recent and renewed effort to free Mazi Nnamdi Kanu from the hostage of APC and its allies from the South-East is a very welcome development. We in the Eastern Union are fully in support and in partnership with the move. The time has come for us to stick out our necks for the worst, otherwise these people that have snatched power will continue to take undue advantage of the people to sustain our enslavement. This present and renewed effort must be sustained until Nnamdi Kanu is released. Tinubu has no right to sustain Buhari's illegality. Tinubu should take steps to release Mazi Nnamdi Kanu before the date set aside for the protests. He should listen to the people because the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

a7469.speaker: Mohamud Abdirahman Sheikh Farah (Beene-Beene), Somali Minister of Planning, Investment and Economic Development
a7469.speech: “This agreement reflects the enduring cooperation between Somalia and the United States, driven by our shared goal of realizing a more resilient, prosperous, and inclusive Somalia” ; “With this support, we will strengthen critical sectors such as education, governance, and economic development to ensure that our people, especially women and youth, have the tools and opportunities to thrive.”

a7469.speaker: Catie Lott, USAID Somalia Mission Director
a7469.speech: “This grant agreement reflects the heart of U.S.-Somalia collaboration. Our partnership focuses on building resilience and stability, stimulating economic growth, enhancing governance, and empowering the future leaders of Somalia.”

a7498.speaker: Social media reports
a7498.speech: alleged a shady fertilizer deal between Salima Sugar Company Limited and Nyasa Hills Company, centering on an upfront payment of K200 million, with some suggesting corruption or mismanagement.

a7498.speaker: In-depth investigation by this publication (Nyasa Times)
a7498.speech: reveals that the transaction, while troubled, was genuine and business-driven, with no sinister agenda behind it.

a7498.speaker: Documents reviewed by this publication (Nyasa Times)
a7498.speech: confirm that Nyasa Hills, in turn, made payments to the Chinese supplier on 25 April 2024.

a7498.speaker: Xingtai Ruijin Import and Export Company, Chinese supplier
a7498.speech: agreed to lift the product but demanded an upfront payment of K200 million to begin the process ; unexpectedly demanded full payment - a staggering K604,293,888 - before releasing the product, contradicting the initial agreement that the fertilizer would be dispatched upon receipt of the quarter payment.

a7498.speaker: Salima Sugar Company Limited (through its retainer lawyers, Chris and Legal)
a7498.speech: demanded the return of the K200 million due to what it viewed as a breach of contract; the law firm is now actively pursuing recovery of the funds on behalf of the company.

a7498.speaker: Wester Peter Kosamu, Counsel, Salima Sugar leadership
a7498.speech: has strongly defended the decision to pursue legal recovery of the K200 million, describing it as a necessary step to protect the company's integrity and safeguard public confidence.
